How much should you offer on a fix and flip? Investors use a quick filter called the seventy percent rule. Here's how it works, and where it can fool you.
Step one, estimate the numbers. The after repair value is what the house will sell for once it's fixed. Here that's two hundred eighty five thousand dollars, and the repairs will cost forty thousand.

Step two, apply the rule. Multiply the after repair value by seventy percent. That's one hundred ninety nine thousand five hundred. Subtract the repairs, forty thousand, and your maximum offer is one hundred fifty nine thousand five hundred dollars.

Step three, remember what the rule ignores. Six months of loan payments, taxes, insurance and utilities add about eleven thousand dollars. Selling costs, at seven percent, add nearly twenty thousand. The rule is a shortcut. It doesn't show your real profit.

Step four, test your offer. At one hundred fifty nine thousand five hundred, profit is about fifty thousand dollars. At one hundred eighty thousand, about twenty nine thousand. At two hundred thousand, only about eight thousand. Every extra dollar you pay comes straight out of your profit.

Step five, test the sale price. If the house only sells for two hundred fifty five thousand, a one hundred eighty thousand dollar offer leaves about one thousand dollars of profit. And the rule's maximum offer drops to one hundred thirty eight thousand five hundred. Always test a lower sale price.
